column1: # Book 5 review (Fable, 2026-10-30). Finding 5.53 accepted: the printed text is "iam mortalibus e divis dare dicta", to give sayings from the gods to mortals themselves; the Opus draft translated an emendation (immortalibus). Secondary 5.72 accepted (vesci = make use of). Secondary 5.58 rejected: aevum has no single fixed rendering and "time" is the sense of aevi leges here. 5.111-112 taken verbatim from the Book 1 review text (1.738-739); 5.128-140 from the Book 3 review text (3.784-796) where the Latin is identical, "Just as" for sicut. 5.31 Thracia is locative. 5.14, 5.64, 5.95, 5.98, 5.103, 5.109, 5.126 brought into the band; 5.68 and 5.129 lengthened to it.

column2: For Ceres is said to have established grain, and Liber
for mortals the liquid of the vine-born juice;
in Thrace, near the Bistonian lands and Ismarus,
Especially since he was used to give, well and divinely,
many sayings from the gods to mortals themselves {{NOTE: the source prints "iam mortalibus e divis"; other editors read "immortalibu' de divis", "about the immortal gods themselves"}}
for the rest, the order of reasoning has now brought me to this,
founded the earth, the sky, the sea, the stars, the sun,
and in what way the human race, with varied speech,
began to make use, among themselves, of the names of things;
one day will give to destruction, and, upheld through many years,
befalls the mind, the coming destruction of heaven and earth,
leads nearest to the human heart and the precincts of the mind.
that all things can be overcome and fall with a dreadful crash.
more holy and with far surer reasoning than
the Pythia, who speaks from the tripod and the laurel of Phoebus, {{NOTE: the priestess of Apollo's oracle at Delphi; repeats 1.739}}
For indeed it cannot be that with any body whatever
the nature of the mind and judgment be thought able to exist.
Just as there can be no tree in the upper air, no clouds {{NOTE: 5.128-141 closely repeat 3.784-797; the English repeats its Book 3 lines where the Latin agrees}}
in the deep sea, nor can fish live in the fields,
nor blood be in wood, nor sap in stones;
it is fixed and ordered where each thing grows and is:
so the nature of the mind cannot arise without the body,
alone, nor exist far off from sinews and blood.
For if it could, the force of the mind itself, much sooner,
could be in the head or shoulders or the lowest heels,
and would be wont to be born in any part you please,
And since even in our body it is evidently fixed
and ordered, it seems, where each can be and grow,
spirit and mind, each apart, all the more must we deny
that, wholly outside the body and the living form,
they could endure in crumbling clods of earth or the sun's fire
